The excerpt is from Boeing’s Annual Report (Item 1 Business and the start of Item 1A Risk Factors) and outlines the company’s structure, markets, offerings, and key risks. It describes Boeing as a major global aerospace firm organized into four segments: Commercial Airplanes (BCA), Defense, Space & Security (BDS), Global Services (BGS), and Boeing Capital (BCC). BCA develops and supports a family of commercial jetliners (737, 747, 767, 777, 787) with ongoing development on 737 MAX derivatives and 777X. BDS focuses on manned and unmanned military aircraft and weapons systems; C4ISR, cyber and intelligence solutions; and space systems (government and commercial satellites, ISS, Commercial Crew, missile defense), with the U.S. Department of Defense as its primary customer (86% of 2018 BDS revenue), plus NASA and international customers. It lists core programs such as F/A-18E/F, F-15, P-8, KC-46A, T-X, CH-47, AH-64, V-22, JDAM, and the ULA joint venture. BGS provides lifecycle services (supply chain, maintenance, modifications, upgrades, spares, training, technical documents, and digital/data analytics). BCC supports customer financing and manages a portfolio of leases, notes, and related assets.

The section covers intellectual property (broad portfolio; no single right is material), workforce (about 153,000 employees; major union representation by IAM, SPEEA, UAW with noted contract expirations), and competition (intense across all segments against Airbus and emerging national entrants; U.S. primes such as Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, General Dynamics, SpaceX; and strong services competitors). It details regulatory and contractual frameworks, including U.S. and non-U.S. government contracting rules and termination rights, FAA and international aviation compliance, environmental obligations and potential PRP liabilities, export/import controls and anti-corruption regulations affecting non-U.S. sales, and risks tied to raw materials (aluminum, titanium, composites), sole-source suppliers, and energy availability. It notes no material seasonality, provides corporate and SEC filing access information, and includes forward‑looking statements cautions.

The beginning of Risk Factors emphasizes BCA and BGS dependence on airline industry dynamics and macroeconomic conditions (traffic growth, profitability, financing, trade policy, geopolitical stability, technology, fuel prices, terrorism, epidemics, environmental rules), the cyclicality of airlines, exposure of multi‑year backlogs to adverse shifts, reliance on a fully operational U.S. Export‑Import Bank for some non‑U.S. financing, and pricing risks from long‑dated, firm fixed‑price aircraft contracts with indexed escalation that may not keep pace with cost increases.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase:

 investment in our common stock or debt securities involves risks and uncertainties and our actual results and future trends may differ materiallyfrom

structure.summary:
- Forward-looking statements safe harbor: outlines that statements about future performance are subject to risks, uncertainties, and may differ materially from actual results; no obligation to update except as required by law.
- Item 1A. Risk Factors:
  - Dependence on commercial airlines and market cyclicality: demand tied to global economic growth, political stability, airline profitability, financing (including U.S. Ex-Im Bank availability), fuel prices, technology, competition, terrorism, epidemics, environmental regulations.
  - Pricing and escalation exposure: firm fixed-price aircraft sales with index-based escalation can compress margins if costs outpace escalation.
  - Customer concentration: significant revenues from a limited number of airlines; fleet decisions, consolidation, or financial distress could reduce sales.
  - Production system and program execution: need to maintain stable production, hit rate targets, and certify/develop new aircraft (e.g., 777X); risks from supplier delays/defects, certification hurdles, out-of-sequence work, higher costs, delivery delays, and increased warranty/support.
  - Performance/reliability risk: failures to meet standards can cause disruptions, higher costs, and lower revenue.
  - U.S. defense spending uncertainty: exposure to changing budgets, priorities, sequestration risks in FY20–FY21, and potential government shutdown impacts (e.g., NASA/FAA); potential effects on programs like F/A-18, CH-47, AH-64, V-22, KC-46A, P-8.
  - Government contracting risks: extensive procurement regulations; potential cost increases and penalties; contracts can be modified, curtailed, or terminated for convenience or default; appropriations/continuing resolution uncertainty; frequent audits (DCAA/DCMA) and potential sanctions, withholds, or debarment.
  - Contract structure risks:
    - Fixed-price contracts (majority at BDS/BGS): margin pressure and reach-forward losses if costs exceed estimates; 2018 charges included KC-46A ($736M), T-X ($400M options), MQ-25 EMD ($291M).
    - Development contracts carry heightened technical/schedule uncertainty (e.g., Commercial Crew, Saudi F-15, KC-46A, T-X, VC-25B, MQ-25, satellites).
    - Cost-type contracts (e.g., GMD, Proprietary, SLS) risk reduced fees or cancellation if issues arise.
    - Satellite in-orbit incentive payments at risk over up to 15 years; failures can trigger revenue reversals/refunds.
  - Supply chain and materials: reliance on U.S. and non-U.S. suppliers, some single-source; disruptions (e.g., 2018 737 supply issues), or shortages/price spikes in aluminum, titanium, composites can delay deliveries and raise costs.
  - Accounting estimates/program accounting: significant judgments on revenues, costs, accounting quantities, pricing, learning curves, escalation, supplier performance, certifications; changes can adversely affect results.
  - Competition: intensifying global competition in commercial jets and defense; consolidation and affordability pressures; BGS faces many of the same competitors.
  - International exposure: 56% of 2018 revenue from non-U.S. customers; risks include regulatory changes, offsets/industrial participation, FX volatility, political/economic instability, financing availability (including Ex-Im), taxes/sanctions/trade controls, complex compliance, and geopolitical events (terrorism, war, epidemics).
  - Cybersecurity: threats to confidentiality, integrity, and availability of Boeing and customer systems; potential financial/reputational harm.
  - Litigation/investigations: unpredictable outcomes could materially affect financial position; significant regulatory oversight.
  - Customer financing concentration: exposure to certain customers, regions, and aircraft types (notably 717 and 747-8); defaults or value declines could harm earnings, cash flows, and financial position.
  - Liquidity/financing: reliance on debt markets; airplane financing commitments of ~$19.5B at 12/31/2018; market disruptions or rating declines could raise costs/limit access.
  - M&A/JVs/divestitures: integration, legacy liability, impairment, and partner risks; KLX Inc. acquisition noted; possible continuing obligations after divestitures.
  - Insurance limitations: certain product liabilities may be uninsurable or inadequately insured; SAFETY Act protections apply only in the U.S.
  - Business disruptions: physical security, IT/cyber incidents, severe weather/natural events, and pandemics can delay production, raise costs, and harm reputation.
  - Labor relations: 35% of workforce (about 54,000 employees) union-represented; risk of strikes and supplier union actions affecting production and development.
  - Pension and OPEB obligations: sensitivity to discount rates and asset returns; effects on expense, cash contributions, shareholders’ equity, and contract profitability (via CAS on U.S. government work).
  - Environmental liabilities: compliance with U.S. and non-U.S. laws; potential cleanup costs, fines, third-party claims; risks from acquired operations and evolving regulations.
- Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments: Not applicable.
- Item 2. Properties:
  - Approximately 87.8–88.0 million sq ft of floor space at 12/31/2018; about 95% in the U.S.
  - By business (thousands of sq ft): Commercial Airplanes ~43,086; Defense, Space & Security ~31,306; Global Services ~8,824; Other ~4,594.
  - Ownership mix (thousands of sq ft): Owned ~69,996; Leased ~17,496; Government-owned ~318 (plus 49 sq ft rent-free).
  - Major locations: 
    - BCA: Greater Seattle, WA; Greater Charleston, SC; Portland, OR; Greater Los Angeles, CA; Greater Salt Lake City, UT; Australia; Canada.
    - BDS: Greater St. Louis, MO; Greater Los Angeles, CA; Greater Seattle, WA; Philadelphia, PA; Mesa, AZ; Huntsville, AL; Oklahoma City, OK; Heath, OH; Greater Washington, DC; Houston, TX.
    - BGS: San Antonio, TX; Greater Miami, FL; Dallas, TX; Germany; Jacksonville, FL; Greater Denver, CO; Mesa, AZ.
    - Other: Chicago, IL; Greater Los Angeles, CA; Greater Seattle, WA; Greater St. Louis, MO; Greater Washington, DC.
  - Use of runways and taxiways on third-party airport properties under long-term municipal and other leases.

structure.summary:
- Management’s Discussion and Analysis covering 2016–2018 consolidated performance, segment strategies, results, liquidity, risks, and critical accounting policies for a global aerospace and defense company with four core businesses: Commercial Airplanes (BCA), Defense, Space & Security (BDS), Global Services (BGS), and Boeing Capital (BCC).
- Consolidated financial highlights:
  - Revenues grew to ~$101.1B in 2018; operating margin improved to 11.9%; effective tax rate down to 9.9%; diluted EPS up to $17.85.
  - Presentation of non-GAAP “core” metrics excluding FAS/CAS service cost adjustment: core operating earnings, margin, and core EPS, with reconciliations.
- Segment revenue and earnings trends:
  - BCA: Revenue up on higher 737 and 787 deliveries and mix; operating margins improved on stronger 787 margins, cost performance, and favorable mix.
  - BDS: Revenue up on non-U.S. fighter awards, weapons, satellites, and final C‑17 sale; earnings down on charges for winning T‑X Trainer and MQ‑25 competitions and higher KC‑46A reach‑forward losses.
  - BGS: Revenue growth across services, notably higher parts (including KLX acquisition); earnings up with some offset from higher period costs.
  - BCC: Smaller portfolio, lower lease income; solid but moderating operating margins.
- KC‑46A Tanker program: Fixed‑price EMD and LRIP status, delivery of first aircraft in Jan 2019, and multi‑year reach‑forward losses in 2016–2018; continued risk of further charges or delays.
- Unallocated items and corporate factors:
  - Variability in deferred compensation linked to market performance.
  - Higher unallocated expenses including R&D timing and a ~$148M Spirit litigation charge.
  - Pension and postretirement cost dynamics (FAS/CAS adjustments) and non‑operating pension impacts.
- Other earnings items: Lower FX gains in 2018, increased interest expense tied to higher debt and lower capitalized interest.
- Costs and R&D:
  - Cost of sales up with volume and development program charges; cost as % of revenue improved.
  - R&D by segment; 2017 decline driven by 2016 787 flight‑test cost reclassification and lower spend on 737 MAX/787‑10/777X; 2018 modest uptick with product development.
- Backlog: Record total backlog ~$490B (contractual and unobligated), with increases led by BDS and services; BCA backlog ~\$412B.
- Global trade and policy environment:
  - Steel/aluminum tariffs and U.S.–China tariff actions; monitoring cost and supply chain impacts.
  - Export‑Import Bank reauthorization but limited by lack of board quorum for large transactions; potential need for alternative customer financing.
  - Russia sanctions monitoring.
- BCA detailed discussion:
  - Industry demand drivers (GDP growth, passenger/cargo traffic), profitability, and risks; competitive landscape (Airbus including A220, Embraer, new entrants in Russia/China/Japan).
  - Deliveries by program; program accounting quantities and firm orders; 737, 747, 767, 777/777X, 787 production rates and plans; 747 viability assessment; fleet support services scope and cost profile.
  - Program development timelines (737 MAX family, 787‑10, 777X) and execution risks (costs, schedules, certification, mix, escalation, claims).
- BDS detailed discussion:
  - U.S. budget dynamics (BBA 2018, shutdown impacts, BCA caps resuming FY20–21) and funding uncertainty; non‑U.S. opportunities (30% of BDS backlog).
  - Platform and satellite deliveries; earnings sensitivity to cumulative catch‑up adjustments; equity earnings from joint ventures (ULA and others).
  - Development program risk profile (cost‑type vs fixed‑price), with exposure on Commercial Crew, KC‑46A, T‑X, MQ‑25, VC‑25B, satellites; specifics on T‑X IDIQ structure and MQ‑25 EMD award with initial reach‑forward losses.
- BGS detailed discussion:
  - Market trends in commercial and government services (parts, logistics, MRO, training, data analytics); competitive pricing pressures.
  - Revenue/earnings growth, margins, and backlog expansion; impact of KLX acquisition.
- BCC overview:
  - Portfolio size/mix, customer credit quality, concentration by aircraft type; potential for increased financing if Ex‑Im remains constrained.
  - Market context (parked aircraft levels) and valuation/lease rate implications; earnings drivers and financial position.
- Liquidity and capital resources:
  - Operating cash flow growth to ~$15.3B in 2018; working capital drivers (advances/progress billings, inventory).
  - Investing: 2018 acquisitions (notably KLX), capex levels and outlook.
  - Financing: Share repurchases (~$9B in 2018), dividends, higher net borrowings, commercial paper usage, available revolving credit capacity (~$5.1B).
  - Financing commitments increased to ~$19.5B; expectation of third‑party financing availability but risk if Ex‑Im constraints persist.
  - Debt levels (~$13.9B), covenant compliance, and ample borrowing capacity; pension underfunding (~$15.3B GAAP) with strong ERISA funding, minimal expected 2019 contributions.
- Contractual obligations and commitments:
  - Schedules for debt and interest, pension/OPEB cash needs, lease obligations, and substantial purchase obligations (recorded and unrecorded).
  - Industrial participation agreements (~$18.4B through 2030); commercial commitments (standby LCs/surety, aircraft financing commitments).
- Contingencies and off‑balance sheet:
  - Legal proceedings, environmental remediation liabilities, guarantees and other off‑balance sheet arrangements.
- Non‑GAAP measures:
  - Definitions and rationale for core operating earnings/margin and core EPS; reconciliation to GAAP and discussion of pension/postretirement components.
- Other compliance:
  - Iran-related activities disclosure (termination/unwind of prior agreements under OFAC license; no revenue/profit).
- Critical accounting policies and sensitivities:
  - Long‑term contract accounting, cumulative catch‑up adjustments and their earnings impact; program accounting methodology and risks (reach‑forward losses), with sensitivity illustrations.
  - Goodwill and indefinite‑lived intangibles impairment testing approach and assumptions.
  - Pension accounting assumptions (discount rate, long‑term asset return) with sensitivity to changes.
- Market risk disclosures (Item 7A):

nodes.title: Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.heading: Note 1 – Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.start_phrase: The Consolidated Financial Statements included in this report have been prepared by management of The Boeing Company (herein referred to as“Boeing,” the “Company,” “we,” “us,” or “our”).
nodes.summary:
- Document type and scope: Boeing’s Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements for years ended December 31, 2018, 2017, and 2016; primarily Note 1 (Summary of Significant Accounting Policies) and Note 2 (Impact of Adoption of New Standards).
- Organization and consolidation: Principles of consolidation for majority-owned subsidiaries and variable interest entities; elimination of intercompany items; reportable segments (BCA, BDS, BGS, BCC) effective July 1, 2017; prior-period reclassifications.
- Estimates and operating cycle: Use of significant estimates under U.S. GAAP; operating cycle based on contract/program duration (often >1 year).
- New accounting standards adopted in 2018 and effects:
  - ASC 606 (ASU 2014-09): Full retrospective adoption; accelerates revenue timing on most defense/services and certain military derivative contracts (revenue recognized as costs are incurred); no change for commercial airplane revenue recognition or program accounting (recognized at delivery). Cumulative impacts: retained earnings +$901 at 1/1/2016; net earnings +$139 (2016) and +$261 (2017).
  - ASU 2017-07 (pension/postretirement presentation): Non-service cost components moved to non-operating income; only service cost capitalized in inventory prospectively (immaterial impact).
  - ASU 2016-18 (restricted cash): Included in cash flow reconciliations (immaterial).
  - ASU 2018-02 (AOCI tax reclassification): Reclass of TCJA effects from AOCI to retained earnings (+$2,997 to both retained earnings and accumulated other comprehensive loss).
- Revenue recognition policies:
  - Commercial aircraft (BCA): Transaction price allocation by standalone selling prices with escalation; revenue at point-in-time on customer acceptance; bill-and-hold possible when transfer-of-control criteria met; program accounting for cost of sales; advances/progress billings customary and not significant financing components.
  - Long-term contracts (BDS, certain BCA/BGS): Typically a single performance obligation; revenue over time via cost-to-complete (percentage-of-completion) due to continuous transfer of control; includes fixed-price and cost-reimbursable arrangements; variable consideration (incentive/award fees) constrained to expected/more-likely amounts; cumulative catch-up adjustments for estimate changes; full reach-forward loss recognition when indicated. Disclosed net cumulative catch-up impacts (2016–2018) and significant KC-46A Tanker reach-forward losses ($1,127 in 2016; $445 in 2017; $736 in 2018).
  - Commercial spare parts (BGS): Point-in-time at delivery; returns considered in transaction price; cost at average cost; prompt payment terms.
  - Other services (BGS): Over-time revenue recognition based on best progress measure (straight-line or billable amounts); cost as incurred.
  - Concession sharing: Customer sales concessions reduce revenue; supplier reimbursements reduce cost of products.
  - Contract assets/liabilities: Definitions of Unbilled receivables (contract assets) and Advances/progress billings (contract liabilities); not significant financing components.
- Financial services and other revenues:
  - Leasing/financing (BCC): Sales-type/finance leases (level yield recognition; residual value estimates); operating leases (straight-line; depreciation to residual); notes receivable interest and discount amortization; residual value impairment recognition if other-than-temporary.
  - Reinsurance: Participation in workers’ compensation reinsurance pool; revenues and costs presented net in cost of sales; amounts disclosed for 2016–2018.
  - Fleet support: Ongoing customer support activities expensed as incurred in cost of services.
- Expense and cost policies:
  - Research and development: Expensed as incurred; bid and proposal costs included; customer-funded best-efforts arrangements offset R&D expense.
  - Share-based compensation: Measured at grant-date fair value for equity-settled; fair value remeasured for cash-settled; expense over requisite service period net of estimated forfeitures.
- Income taxes: Current/deferred taxes; accounting for uncertain tax positions (more-likely-than-not); recognition of interest/penalties in tax expense.
- Postretirement and postemployment:
  - Pension/OPEB: Transition to defined contribution for many employees; measurement assumptions (discount rate, expected return, medical trend); partial capitalization of service cost to inventory pre-2018; actuarial gains/losses in equity with amortization thresholds; funded status on balance sheet.
  - Postemployment benefits: Liability recognized when probable and estimable for vested/accumulated rights.
- Contingencies and environmental: Accruals for probable and estimable environmental remediation; recoveries recognized when probable; undiscounted liabilities due to timing uncertainty.
- Cash and cash equivalents: Highly liquid instruments with maturities ≤3 months; bank balance netting with right of set-off; negative balances reclassified to accounts payable.
- Inventories and program accounting:
  - Inclusion of direct costs, tooling, overhead within NRV limits; abnormal or non-attributable fixed costs expensed; long-cycle amounts may extend beyond one year.
  - Commercial programs: Deferred production costs (learning curve/volume efficiencies) and supplier advances; quarterly program reviews for NRV; program loss provisions when EAC indicates loss; spare parts at lower of average cost or NRV with impairment for excess/obsolete; early issue sales consideration recorded as revenue reduction at delivery (recoverability assessed if non-performance); used aircraft at lower of cost/NRV (may be leased temporarily).
  - Government contracts: Allowable reengineering costs included.
  - Precontract costs: Capitalized if probable of recovery; otherwise expensed or written off.
- Property, plant and equipment: Historical cost less depreciation; methods/lives (buildings 10–40 yrs, 150% DB; machinery/equipment 4–20 yrs, SYD); internal-use software amortized straight-line (typically 5 yrs); impairment testing for held-for-use and held-for-sale assets.
- Asset retirement obligations: Recognized when fair value estimable; conditional obligations recorded when estimable; undiscovered obligations not recognized until identified.
- Goodwill and intangibles: Annual impairment testing (April 1) or upon triggering events; qualitative or two-step goodwill test; indefinite-lived intangibles tested via discounted cash flows; finite-lived intangibles amortized over stated ranges and tested for recoverability/impairment.
- Investments: Time deposits (held-to-maturity at cost); available-for-sale debt at fair value with OCI; equity method for significant influence; other equity at fair value through earnings or at cost adjusted for observable changes; operating vs non-operating investment income classification.
- Derivatives and hedging: All derivatives at fair value; accounting for fair value and cash flow hedges; ineffectiveness to earnings; certain aluminum purchase/sale agreements treated as derivatives without hedge accounting; non-designated derivatives to earnings.
- Aircraft valuation and customer financing:
  - Trade-in and contingent repurchase commitments: Revenue adjustments and cost charges based on fair value vs contractual trade-in price; estimation processes and valuation sources; exposure recognition in accrued liabilities.
  - Used aircraft valuation, placement markets (resale, leasing, scrap), and quarterly revaluation.
  - Customer financing portfolio: Operating lease equipment, sales-type/finance leases, and notes; fair value assessment, impairment testing, and allowance for losses framework using collateral values, customer credit ratings, default rates, and contract terms; ability to look beyond specific collateral under certain agreements.
- Warranties and performance guarantees: Standard BCA and BDS warranty terms; accrual methodologies based on coverage months and historical claims; additional accruals for fleet-wide issues; performance guarantees treated as warranties with revenue reductions; supplier recoveries recorded to inventory/cost reduction.
- Supplier penalties: Accrued when probable and estimable.
- Guarantees: Fair value recognition for guarantees issued/modified; measurement approach and treatment of probable contingent losses.
- Standards issued but not yet implemented: ASC 842 Leases to be adopted prospectively on January 1, 2019; expected to have no material impact on financial position, results, or cash flows.
- Quantitative restatement impacts (Note 2): Presentation of 2016–2017 restated results reflecting adoption of ASC 606, ASU 2017-07, ASU 2016-18, and ASU 2018-02, including line-item effects on revenues, costs, earnings from operations, other income, taxes, net earnings, and EPS.

structure.summary:
- Signatures for The Boeing Company’s 2018 Form 10-K, executed February 8, 2019, pursuant to the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, including signature by Robert E. Verbeck (Senior Vice President, Finance and Corporate Controller) and a signature block for officers and directors such as Dennis A. Muilenburg (Chairman, President and CEO), Gregory D. Smith (CFO and EVP), and directors Lynn J. Good, Lawrence W. Kellner, Caroline B. Kennedy, Robert A. Bradway, Edward M. Liddy, David L. Calhoun, Susan C. Schwab, Arthur D. Collins, Jr., Ronald A. Williams, Kenneth M. Duberstein, Mike S. Zafirovski, and Edmund P. Giambastiani, Jr.
- Exhibit 21: Partial list of significant subsidiaries and jurisdictions (e.g., Aviall Services, Inc.; Boeing Capital Corporation; Boeing Aircraft Holding Company; Boeing Europe B.V.; Boeing Defence Australia Ltd; Jeppesen Sanderson, Inc.; Insitu, Inc.; KLX Inc.; various entities in Delaware, Germany, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Australia, Bermuda, and Washington). Statement that non-significant subsidiaries are omitted in accordance with SEC rules.
- Exhibit 23: Deloitte & Touche LLP consent to incorporation by reference of their audit reports into specified S-8 and S-3 registration statements. The audit reports (dated February 8, 2019, Chicago, Illinois) include an unqualified opinion with an explanatory paragraph on Boeing’s change in revenue recognition method and an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting.
- Exhibits 31.1 and 31.2: Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 certifications by the CEO (Dennis A. Muilenburg) and CFO (Gregory D. Smith) affirming review of the 10-K, accuracy and fair presentation of the financial statements, design and evaluation of disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting, disclosure of changes to internal controls, and communication of significant deficiencies, material weaknesses, and fraud to auditors and the audit committee.
- Exhibits 32.1 and 32.2: Sarbanes-Oxley Section 906 certifications by the CEO and CFO stating the 10-K complies with Section 13(a) or 15(d) of the Exchange Act and fairly presents, in all material respects, the company’s financial condition and results of operations. All dated February 8, 2019.
